title: Narc
full_review:
Narc" (Paramount) is a gritty morality tale exploring the tenuous boundary separating justice from vengeance and the hazards posed by blurring the distinctions between the two.

Director Joe Carnahan's foray into the dark, often brutal world of undercover narcotics operations centers on detective Nick Tellis (Jason Patric), a burnout case reluctantly drawn back onto the force to solve the murder of a young police officer killed in the line of duty. A compelling story, buttressed by solid performances and dynamic pacing, infuses the film with a raw immediacy, although the recurring explicit violence may prove more than a little off-putting.

Tellis is a man on the edge. A three-year tour of duty as a member of the Detroit Police Department's undercover narcotics unit has afforded him a front-row view of the ugly underbelly of the Motor City's drug scene. Suspended from the force for the accidental shooting of a pregnant woman (graphically depicted) while in pursuit of a low-level dealer, Tellis is an emotional time-bomb waiting to explode. Having had to straddle the ideological fence for so long in order to survive on the streets, he is no longer certain to which side he will ultimately gravitate.

Haunted by inner demons and supporting a wife and child, he is not anxious to return to the trenches. However, when brought up before a review board, Tellis is offered a deal -- help them crack a homicide case involving a murdered cop, Michael Calvess (Alan Van Sprang), and they will dismiss all charges and secure him a cushy, desk job far from the front lines. Though averse at first, Tellis agrees, with one stipulation: they allow him to enlist the aid of the slain officer's volatile partner, Det. Henry Oak (Ray Liotta), a brass-knuckles, old-school veteran obsessed with avenging Calvess' murder.

Despite his wife's concern for his physical and psychological well-being, Tellis sees the investigation as an opportunity to exorcise his self-loathing, proving that, despite past indiscretions, he is different from the detritus that mires him. His marriage eroding, Tellis immerses himself deeper and deeper into the belly of the beast. Relentlessly, the two rogue cops chase down leads, track informants, all the while zeroing in on the truth about both the murder and their own secret sins.

Cinematographer Alex Nepomniaschy's bleakly monochromatic streets mirror an equally barren inner landscape, one devoid of any clear-cut black and white but awash in shades of gray. Both the cerebral Tellis and the emotive Oak are good men, each driven by strong moral convictions, but compelled to operate in a cold, Darwinian universe, utilizing ignoble means to achieve noble ends.

Carnahan has created a morally ambiguous world where objective "good" and "evil" are relegated to dangerous luxuries, currencies with little street value. Despite the film's relativistic tone, the climax does pronounce a judgment, though it is more reflective of a Greek tragedy where the Fates exact a price for some character's fatal flaw, rather than offer a spirit of Christian redemption.

In weaving his grim, multilayered tapestry, Carnahan has borrowed heavily from past films. The exploration of the elusive nature of truth in "Narc" echoes "Rashomon," even mimicking its technique of showing the same incident from varying perspectives, resulting in a structurally intriguing narrative, albeit one that is at times oblique. The film's gritty realism and underlying theme of "the good man trapped in a corrupt system" are reminiscent of such 1970s classics as "The French Connection" and "Serpico."

Due to some graphic violence, much rough language and profanities, and recurring drug content, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
